summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe temporary colour service: consult with the client, do the skin and strand tests the manufacturer asks for, check the scalp, use the colour wheel to choose a shade, protect the client and yourself, and apply rinses, mousses, gels, sprays and hair mascara evenly on straight, relaxed, natural and loc'd hair. You will also learn to handle and store colour products safely, give aftercare advice, clean up and keep records.

blocks.p: Temporary colour is the gentlest colour service a salon offers: a colour that sits on the outside of the hair and washes out at the next shampoo. It is used to tone a shade, blend a little grey, add shine, or give a bright, bold look for a carnival, a school event, a party or a photo shoot. Because it is gentle, it is the first colour service you learn. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees.

Gentle does not mean careless. A temporary colour can still cause an allergic reaction, sting broken skin, stain skin and clothes, and look patchy if it is put on badly. In this unit you learn to **consult, test, protect, apply evenly and advise**, and those habits will carry you into semi-permanent and permanent colour later.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the first you consult, strand test and apply a colour rinse on a training head with textured hair. In the second you plan and create a creative colour look for an event on natural or textured hair with at least two kinds of temporary colour, then show that it washes out. The assessor watches your tests, protection, sectioning, evenness, safety with sprays, clean-up and record card.

sections.title: How colour products work on the hair

blocks.p: A hair has three layers. The **cuticle** is the outer layer of overlapping scales. Under it is the **cortex**, which holds the hair's natural pigment, **melanin**, and gives the hair its strength. In the centre is the medulla. Where a colour product's molecules end up decides how long it lasts.

head: Type of colour
Where it works
Developer?
Can it lighten?
How long it lasts
Examples
rows: Temporary
Large colour molecules **coat the outside** of the cuticle.
No
No
Until the next shampoo (one wash)
Colour rinse, mousse, gel, spray, hair mascara, chalk, shampoo-in colour
Semi-permanent
Smaller molecules slip **a little way under the cuticle**, into the edge of the cortex.

Fades over several shampoos, as the maker says
Colour glosses and 'wash-out' colours
Permanent
Mixed with **developer (hydrogen peroxide)**; opens the cuticle and forms large colour molecules inside the cortex.
Yes
Yes (and darken)
Until it grows out or is cut; regrowth shows

blocks.p: Because a temporary colour only adds colour on top, it **cannot lighten**: a client with dark brown hair cannot be made blonde for one night with a rinse or a spray. On dark hair, a bright temporary colour shows as a tint or sheen; on light, grey or pre-lightened hair it shows strongly.

blocks.h: Why a temporary colour sometimes stays

blocks.p: On hair that is very **porous** (lightened, bleached, over-relaxed, heat-damaged, or the dry ends of coily hair), the cuticle is raised and the colour can get under it and hold on as a stain that lasts several washes. A strand test shows whether this will happen. Warn the client before you colour porous or grey hair with a strong shade.

blocks.note: Use each product exactly as its maker says. **Never mix products from different brands**, and never add one product to another to 'make it stronger': you do not know what is in them, and the result can be uneven, sticky or harmful.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Colour theory for choosing a shade

blocks.p: Hair colour theory uses the painter's colour wheel. The three **primary colours** are **red, yellow and blue**; every other colour is mixed from them. Mixing two primaries gives the **secondary colours**: red + yellow = orange, yellow + blue = green, blue + red = violet. On the wheel, each secondary colour sits opposite the primary that is not in it.

head: Unwanted tone in the hair
Its complementary colour (opposite on the wheel)
What to use
rows: Yellow (a 'brassy' blonde, or yellowed grey or white hair)
Violet
A violet-based rinse, mousse or toning shampoo
Orange (dark hair that was lightened, now 'rusty')
Blue
A blue-based toner or rinse
Red (red hair fading warm, or unwanted red in brown hair)
Green
A green- or ash-based toner

blocks.p: Colours opposite each other on the wheel are **complementary colours**: put together, they **neutralise** (cancel) each other and the result looks more natural. This is how a temporary rinse 'tones' hair. It does not lighten or remove the unwanted tone; it covers it with its opposite so that the eye no longer sees it.

blocks.note: Toning works in small amounts. Too much violet on yellow hair does not give 'more neutral': it gives lilac hair. Use the maker's timing, and do a strand test on porous hair.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Depth (level)** is how light or dark a colour is. Natural hair is usually described on a scale from **1 (black)** to **10 (lightest blonde)**, with dark brown around 3 to 4, medium brown 5, light brown 6, and blondes 7 to 10.
**Tone** is the shade you see within that depth: warm tones such as gold, copper and red; cool tones such as ash and violet; and neutral.
A temporary colour cannot change the depth upwards. It can add tone, deepen slightly, or add a bright colour over a light base.

blocks.h: Choosing the shade with the client

ul: Use the maker's **shade chart** in good, natural or daylight-type light, never under a coloured or dim lamp.

Look at the chart against the client's own hair, and **agree the shade together**. Explain how it will show on her depth of hair: a bright blue spray will shine on black hair but will not turn it blue.
Ask what the colour is for and how long it needs to last. A carnival costume, a school colour day and a grandmother toning her grey need different products.
Say what the product can and cannot do, before you start, so that she is not disappointed.

blocks.p: Sit the client in good light and talk face to face. Even a one-night colour needs a proper consultation, because the skin can react to any colour product and the hair's history changes how colour takes.

head: Ask or look at
Why
rows: What she wants, and the occasion
Chooses the product and shade, and how long it must last.
Past colour, lightener, relaxer, texturiser, perm, henna and home products, and when
Porous or treated hair takes colour differently and may hold a stain. Some home products can react with salon chemicals.
Any allergy, sensitive skin, or a past reaction to a hair or skin product
Points to the need for a skin test, or to a product to avoid. A past reaction is a warning that goes on the record.
The hair: natural depth, grey, porosity, condition, curl pattern
Decides how the colour will show, whether a strand test is needed, and how gently to work.
The scalp and hairline: cuts, scratches, sores, flaking, swelling, infection
Finds contra-indications before any product touches the skin.
What the maker's instructions require
Which tests are needed and when; what hair state the product goes on; any timing.

blocks.p: Explain that a temporary colour adds colour on top, cannot lighten, washes out at the next shampoo, and can rub off or run. Agree the shade, the plan and the price, and write it on the **record card**.

A skin (patch) test checks whether the client is **allergic** to the product. Not every temporary product needs one, but you must do one **whenever the manufacturer's instructions say so**, and you may never skip it because 'it's only temporary'. The maker also says how far ahead to do it (often **48 hours**) and where (usually behind the ear or in the crook of the elbow).

flow: Clean a small area of skin
Gloves on; apply a little product with a cotton bud
Tell her what to watch for
Check at the time the maker gives

ul: **Negative**: the skin looks normal. Record it and go ahead.

**Positive**: redness, itching, swelling, soreness, a rash or blisters. **Do not apply the colour.** Record it, tell your supervisor and advise her to see a doctor. A different shade of the same product is still the same product.
If the maker asks for a test before every service, or after a gap, do it again.

blocks.p: A strand test is done on a small section of the **hair**, often at the nape, or on a cutting of hair, using the product as the maker says. It shows what the colour will look like on her hair, how long to leave it where a time is given, and whether porous or lightened hair will **hold a stain**. On locs it also shows whether the product will **rinse out**. If the result is poor, change the product, the shade or the plan.

head: What you find
What you do
rows: Cuts, scratches or abrasions on the scalp or hairline (from scratching, tight braids, a comb)
Do not colour today. Colour stings and can get into broken skin and cause a reaction or infection. Rebook once the skin has healed.
Ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis: round, scaly patches, broken hairs), impetigo (weeping, yellow-crusted sores), head lice
No service. These spread to other clients. Refer her to a doctor or pharmacist; clean and disinfect everything used.
A positive skin test, or a past reaction to hair colour
Do not use the product. Record it; advise a doctor.
A very red, swollen or sore scalp, or a scalp under a doctor's treatment
Do not colour. Check with the supervisor; ask whether her doctor has cleared salon services.
Very porous, damaged hair
Not a reason to stop, but a strand test is needed and the client is warned that the colour may stay longer.

blocks.note: Tell the client privately and kindly what you can see and why you cannot colour today. Do not diagnose, do not name a disease you are not sure of, and do not try to work around it. Record what you found.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Preparing the area, the client and yourself

ul: Clean and disinfect the station. Set out clean, disinfected tools: tint bowl, applicator bottle or brush, wide-tooth comb, tail comb, sectioning clips, a timer, and a towel for wiping.
Check the product: the **right product, the agreed shade, in date**, lid and nozzle clean. Read the instructions again.
Have the record card with the test results in front of you.
**Ventilate** the area, especially for sprays: open windows, use the extractor fan, or work where air moves. Keep sprays away from other clients.
Keep a bin for used gloves and paper, and a wet cloth or stain remover ready for skin.

flow: Barrier cream on hairline and ears
Shampoo and towel-dry, or dry and style, as the product needs

ul: Gown her, put a towel round her shoulders and a **waterproof colour cape** over it. Temporary colour stains clothes, and some do not wash out of fabric.
Apply **barrier cream** along the hairline, over the tops of the ears and at the nape. It stops colour staining the skin. Keep it off the hair, where it would block the colour.

Prepare the hair as the maker says. Most **rinses and mousses** go on **shampooed, towel-dried** hair that is damp but not dripping, so that the colour spreads evenly and does not run. **Sprays, hair mascara and chalk** go on **dry, styled** hair at the end.
Explain each step as you go and check she is comfortable.
Wash your hands. Wear **disposable gloves**: colour stains and can irritate the skin, and gloves also keep germs off the client's scalp.
Wear an **apron** to protect your clothes. Tie back long hair.
Do not eat, drink or use your phone during the service.

blocks.note: Keep every electrical tool (dryer, hood dryer, flat iron) away from the basin and away from aerosol sprays. Jamaica's supply is 110 V, 50 Hz; dry your hands before touching a plug.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Colour rinse or mousse, step by step

flow: Divide into four sections and clip
Apply section by section, roots to ends
Wipe any colour off the skin at once
Time it, if the maker gives a time
Style, or rinse, as the maker says

ul: Divide the hair into **four sections** (front to nape, ear to ear) and clip them. Work on one at a time, taking thin sub-sections.

Apply from the applicator bottle, a brush or your gloved fingers, from **roots to ends** on each sub-section, and **comb through** with a wide-tooth comb so that every strand is coated. Missed strands and uneven amounts are what make a result **patchy**.
Keep colour off the scalp where you can, and wipe drips on the skin straight away with a damp cloth; wet colour comes off, dried colour stains.
Where the maker gives a time, set the **timer** and keep to it. Where the product is not rinsed out (most rinses), go straight on to the set or blow-dry.
If the product is to be rinsed, rinse with lukewarm water until it runs clear, and towel-blot gently.
Use sprays on **dry, finished** hair, as the last step, so that combing and brushing do not take the colour off again.
Shake the can as the label says. Hold it at the **distance the maker gives** (often about 15 to 20 cm). Too close gives wet, drippy patches; too far gives a thin, uneven mist.
**Shield the client's face** with your hand, a towel or a face shield, and ask her to close her eyes and mouth. Protect her clothing and the station.
Spray in short bursts, moving the can, and build the colour up in light layers rather than one heavy coat.
Work in a **ventilated** area so that nobody breathes the spray. Never spray near a flame, a hot tool or a hood dryer.
Hair mascara: brush it along single strands on dry hair, from a little away from the scalp to the ends. Good for a few grey hairs at the hairline, or fine streaks.
Gel: work it through small, damp or dry sections with gloved fingers, then shape the twist, coil or edge. Let it dry before the client touches it.
Chalk: dampen the strand, rub or press the chalk along it, let it dry and seal with a light hairspray. It comes off on hands and clothes more than other products, so warn the client.

blocks.p: A temporary rinse does not cover grey the way a permanent colour does. It **blends or tones** it: a darker rinse makes the grey less noticeable until the next shampoo, and a violet- or silver-based rinse takes the yellow out of grey and white hair. Grey hair can be porous and may take a strong shade more deeply than the client expects, so strand test first.

ul: Coily hair is often **drier and more porous in places**, especially at the ends, so it can take colour **unevenly**. Do a strand test, and work in **small sections** so that the colour reaches every coil.
Detangle gently first, with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb, from the ends up. Never drag a fine comb through coily hair to spread colour.
Gels, mousses, hair mascara and sprays suit twists, coils, puffs and defined curls, and need no heat. Avoid heavy brushing, pulling and high heat on fragile hair.
Protect the **hairline and edges**: they are often fine and break easily.

On **locs**, check with a strand test that the product will **rinse out**. Colour, gel and residue can build up inside a loc and stay there. Lighter products, sprays and rinses are usually safer than thick gels; follow the maker's advice for locs.
Dry or style the hair as agreed, then look at it in **good light** from the front, both sides and the back.
Look for patches, missed strands, drips on the skin and colour on the cape or collar.
Show the client in the mirror, with a hand mirror for the back, and **ask what she thinks**. If something needs fixing, do it now, not after she has left.

head: Problem
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Patchy, uneven colour
Sections too big, colour not combed through, hair too wet or too dry, product uneven
Re-apply to the pale areas and comb through; next time take smaller sections
Colour on the skin at the hairline or ears
Barrier cream missed or too thin; drips not wiped
Remove gently with a stain remover or the maker's wipe, as its instructions say; never scrub the skin
Colour too strong, or an odd shade
Hair more porous than expected; no strand test; wrong product for her depth
Shampoo it out; choose a lighter shade or a different product and strand test
Colour runs or drips
Hair too wet; too much product; spray held too close
Blot, re-apply more lightly; let each layer of spray dry
Colour will not wash out of some strands
Very porous, lightened or damaged hair has held a stain
Clarifying shampoo and conditioning; it fades with further washes; warn clients beforehand

sections.title: Safe handling, storage and first aid

blocks.p: Every chemical product sold to salons comes with a **safety data sheet (SDS)** from the manufacturer. It tells you the product's **hazards** (for example, flammable, irritant), how to **handle and store** it safely, what protective equipment to wear, what to do with spills, and the **first aid** for skin, eyes and swallowing. Know where the salon keeps its SDS file, and read the sheet for any product you are not sure about.

ul: Keep every product in its **original, labelled container** with the lid closed. Never decant colour into unlabelled bottles.
Store in a **cool, dry place**, out of direct sunlight and away from heat. Jamaica's heat spoils products and can burst cans; a shelf by a window or near a hood dryer is a bad place.

**Aerosol sprays** are stored **upright**, away from heat, flames, hot tools and dryers. The contents are under pressure and usually flammable. Never pierce or burn a can, even an 'empty' one; dispose of cans as the salon's rules say.
Keep products out of the reach of children, and away from the drinks and food area.
Use the oldest stock first; check dates. Report damaged, leaking or swollen containers and do not use them.
Only in a **well-ventilated** area, so that nobody breathes in the spray; the mist irritates the lungs and the eyes.
Never near a lit cigarette, a candle, a stove, a hot flat iron or a hood dryer: the spray can catch fire.
Shield the client's face; keep spray away from everyone's eyes and mouth; warn other clients and staff nearby.
Wipe spray off the floor at once: it makes tiles slippery.

head: If...
What you do
rows: Colour gets into an eye
**Rinse at once** with plenty of clean, cool running water, holding the eyelid open, for the time the SDS says (often at least 10 to 15 minutes)
Tilt the head so that the water runs away from the other eye
Do not let her rub it
If it stays sore, red or blurred, get medical help
Record the accident
Colour on the skin stings or burns
Rinse with plenty of water; stop the service if the skin is reacting; tell the supervisor
Swelling of the face, lips or throat, difficulty breathing, after a colour product
This is a severe allergic reaction: call **110** for an ambulance and tell the supervisor at once
Spray breathed in; coughing or wheezing
Move her to fresh air; get help if it does not settle
Product swallowed (a child)
Do not make him vomit; read the SDS; get medical help and take the container with you

blocks.note: Report every accident, however small, in the salon's accident book, with the date, the person, what happened and what was done.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: The colour sits on the **outside** of the hair and will wash out at the next shampoo. If she wants it gone sooner, she shampoos; if she wants it longer, she waits to wash.
It can **rub off** on pillowcases, collars, towels, hats and hands. Suggest a dark pillowcase or a satin scarf or bonnet at night.

It can **run** in heavy rain, sea water, the pool, a sweaty session at the gym or a hot carnival road. Suggest an umbrella, a cap or a shower cap, and tell her not to be alarmed by coloured water when she washes.
On very porous or lightened hair, some colour may stay for a few washes; explain how to wash it out gently with a mild or clarifying shampoo and a conditioner.
Natural hair: moisturise after the colour is washed out; gels and sprays can be drying.
If the scalp itches, burns or swells, she should shampoo the product out and contact the salon or a doctor.

flow: Gloves still on: wipe the station
Rinse tint bowls, brushes and bottles
Wash tools in warm, soapy water
Linen to the laundry; gloves and papers to the bin
Lids on; products back to storage

ul: **Cleaning** removes colour, hair and dirt with detergent and water. **Disinfecting** then kills most germs with a chemical. Cleaning always comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt.
Bowls, brushes and bottles are washed clean, then disinfected as the label says, before they are used on the next client.
Used towels, gowns and capes go to the laundry; colour-stained linen is washed separately.
Wipe the chair, the basin and the floor; put out a wet floor sign while the floor dries.

head: Record
Example
rows: Date, stylist, service
14 June; trainee Keisha; temporary colour rinse and set
Consultation findings
Natural depth 2, about 20% grey at the front; medium porosity; relaxed 6 weeks ago; no allergies reported
Tests
Skin test 12 June, behind right ear, as the maker requires: negative. Strand test at nape: even take, no staining

The product's name and the shade, exactly as on the label
Timing
Any time the maker gave and the time used

Even result; slight stain at left ear removed with stain remover
Advice given
Washes out at next shampoo; may rub off on pillow; satin scarf at night

blocks.p: Good records let the next stylist repeat a result, avoid a product that caused a problem, and show what was done if there is a complaint. Keep them private: in a closed file or a password-protected system.

ul: I can explain how temporary, semi-permanent and permanent colour work on the hair and how long each lasts.
I can explain why a temporary colour cannot lighten hair.

I can recognise the contra-indications to colouring and tell the client tactfully.
I can prepare the area, gown and protect the client, apply barrier cream, and protect myself.
I can apply a rinse or mousse evenly in sections and comb it through.

I can colour natural, coily and loc'd hair with extra care.
I can check the result, correct patchiness and remove skin stains.
I can use a safety data sheet, store aerosols safely, and give first aid for colour in the eye.
I can give aftercare advice, clean and disinfect tools, and fill in the record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, name the maker's instructions as your guide for tests, hair state, timing and distance, and give the reason for each step.
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: Carnival colours in Kingston
c1.text: Trainee Keisha is preparing a temporary colour look for Carnival for her client Alicia Reid, 23, at a salon in Kingston. Alicia has natural coily hair, worn in chunky twists, with ends that are much drier and rougher than the roots. She wants bright turquoise on the twists and some glitter spray to finish. The maker's leaflet for the gel does not require a skin test; the leaflet for the spray says to hold the can about 15 cm from the hair. The salon's windows are closed and the air conditioning is off.

c2.title: Toning Mrs. Ellis's grey in Brown's Town
c2.text: Mrs. Icilda Ellis, 68, visits a salon in Brown's Town for a shampoo and roller set. Her hair is about half grey, and the grey has turned yellowish. She asks trainee Damian whether 'something can be done about the yellow' without a permanent colour, because she has had a rash from hair dye before. The rinse Damian plans to use says on its leaflet that a skin test is required 48 hours before use. She comes in on Monday; the set is booked for Thursday.

c3.title: A school colour day in Spanish Town
c3.text: Mrs. Jackson brings her daughters, Shania, 15, and Renée, 10, to a salon in Spanish Town on Friday afternoon for red streaks for their school's colour day on Monday. Shania's hair was lightened at the ends by a friend last month and feels very rough. Renée has a few small scratches at her nape from scratching mosquito bites. Trainee Oneika is doing both services with a colour rinse.

c4.title: Locs for a wedding in Montego Bay
c4.text: Mr. Lloyd Grant, 40, has shoulder-length locs and is a groomsman at a wedding in Montego Bay on Saturday. He wants a dark burgundy on his locs for the day only. Trainee Shantol has a thick colour gel and a colour spray available. The salon is busy, and a hood dryer is running at the next station.

c5.title: The end of a long day in Portmore
c5.text: At 6:30 p.m. in a salon in Portmore, trainee Ricardo has finished a colour rinse and blow-dry on a client. There is a brown stain on the skin in front of her left ear. The tint bowl and brush are in the basin with colour drying on them. A half-used can of colour spray is lying on its side on the counter under the hood dryer, and the SDS folder has fallen on the floor. As he wipes the counter, a splash of leftover rinse flicks into his own eye.

questions.q: Why should Keisha do a strand test on Alicia's hair before the turquoise gel, even though the maker does not ask for a skin test?
o: A strand test is the legal replacement for a skin test on natural hair
The dry, porous ends may take the colour unevenly or hold a stain
Coily hair is always resistant, so the gel needs testing for strength
The glitter spray cannot be used until a strand test has been passed
questions.why: The strand test is about the hair, not the skin. Coily hair is often drier and more porous at the ends, so the colour can take unevenly or stain porous areas; the test shows this before the whole head is done.

questions.q: How should Keisha work the gel into the twists?
o: With a fine-tooth comb dragged through each twist from root to end
On the surface of each twist only, so that the ends are not wet
In small sections with gloved fingers, so that every coil is coated
On dry hair after the glitter spray, so the gel seals the glitter
questions.why: Small sections and gloved fingers (or a wide-tooth comb) get colour into every coil without breaking fragile hair. Fine combs drag and snap coily hair, and sprays are the last step, not the first.

questions.q: What should Keisha do before she uses the glitter spray?
o: Warm the can under the hood dryer so that the glitter flows evenly
Spray a test burst at the next station to see how fine the mist is
Open the windows or turn on the extractor, and shield Alicia's face
Hold the can close, about 5 cm away, to keep the spray off the floor
questions.why: Sprays are used in a ventilated area so nobody breathes the mist, with the face shielded, at the maker's distance (here 15 cm). Heat makes cans burst, and spraying near others is unsafe.

questions.q: What should Keisha tell Alicia about her colour on the road on Carnival day?
o: It will have set hard by then and cannot run, however hot the day is
It may run in sweat and rain and rub off on her costume
It will last through several washes, so she need not plan to wash it out
She should wash it out the night before so that it looks fresher on the day
questions.why: Temporary colour sits on the outside of the hair and runs in sweat, rain and water and rubs off on fabric. The client should know this before the event.

questions.q: Which kind of rinse would tone down the yellow in Mrs. Ellis's grey hair?
o: A blue-based rinse
A violet-based rinse
A green-based rinse
A gold-based rinse
questions.why: Violet sits opposite yellow on the colour wheel, so a violet-based product neutralises yellow. Blue cancels orange, green cancels red, and gold would add more warmth.

questions.q: Mrs. Ellis has had a rash from hair dye before, and the rinse requires a skin test. If Damian does the test on Monday afternoon, can the set go ahead on Thursday?
o: No, because a past rash means a rinse may never be used on her
Yes, if the test is checked and is negative, and the result recorded
Yes, and no test is needed, as a rinse is not a permanent colour
No, because a skin test must be done on the same day as the service
questions.why: The maker requires a test 48 hours ahead; Monday to Thursday is more than 48 hours. The service goes ahead only if the result is negative. A past reaction makes the test more important, not optional.

questions.q: On Thursday the test area is normal. Damian applies the violet rinse and, to be sure the yellow goes, leaves it on for twice the time on the leaflet. What is the likely result?
o: The yellow is removed completely and the hair is a cleaner white
No difference, as a temporary colour cannot be left on too long
The grey takes on a lilac tint because the toner has gone too far
The rinse lightens the grey hair because it has worked for longer
questions.why: Toning cancels yellow in small amounts; too much violet, or too long, tints grey and porous hair lilac. A temporary colour cannot lighten, and the maker's timing is there to be followed.

questions.q: What should Damian write on Mrs. Ellis's record card about the test?
o: 'Test done, OK' beside the service, as the detail is in the leaflet
The date, the product, the place on the skin and the negative result
Only the product name, since a negative test need not be recorded
Her past rash, and a note that she should not have colour again
questions.why: A test is recorded with the date, the product, where it was placed and the result, so that the next stylist knows it was done and was clear. A past rash is noted as history, not as a ban on tested products.

questions.q: Oneika slides her fingers along Shania's lightened ends and they feel very rough. What should she tell Mrs. Jackson before she colours them?
o: The red may stay in the porous ends for several washes, not just one
The red will not take at all on lightened hair, so the ends will stay pale
The ends must be cut off before any colour can be applied to the hair
The colour will be lighter on the ends than on the rest of the hair
questions.why: Lightened, rough hair is very porous: it soaks up the colour and may hold a stain after the first shampoo. The client is warned before the service, and a strand test shows how strong the effect will be.

questions.q: What should Oneika do about Renée's scratched nape?
o: Colour the top and sides only, keeping the rinse well away from the nape
Put barrier cream over the scratches and colour as planned
Not colour Renée today, and offer a date once the skin has healed
Colour as planned, but rinse the nape with cool water straight after
questions.why: Colour on broken skin stings and can cause a reaction or infection, so the service waits until the skin has healed. Working around or covering the area still risks product reaching it on a wriggling child.

questions.q: Renée is only 10. Apart from her nape, what else should Oneika have checked before planning a colour for her?
o: That her hair is at least shoulder length, so there is enough to colour
That she has had a permanent colour before, so the hair is used to it
That the school has sent a letter agreeing to red streaks on a pupil
That the product's age limit and the salon's policy allow it, with consent
questions.why: Many colour products carry a minimum age, and a child needs a parent's or guardian's consent and the salon's agreement. The other options are not requirements for a colour service.

questions.q: Oneika finishes Shania's streaks and the colour looks uneven, darker in some places than others. What is the most likely reason?
o: Red is a primary colour, so it can never go on evenly without a developer
The rinse was not combed through evenly, and the porous ends took more
The hair was too dry for a rinse, so only the roots took any of the colour
The barrier cream was put on the hair as well as the hairline
questions.why: Patchy colour comes from uneven application, missed strands and differences in porosity. Primary colours do not need developer, and barrier cream on the hair would block colour, not deepen it.

questions.q: Which is the better product choice for Mr. Grant's locs, and why?
o: The thick gel, because it holds the colour inside the loc for the whole wedding day
The spray or a lighter product, once a strand test shows it rinses out
The gel, because sprays cannot be used on locs under any circumstances
Either, because temporary colour always washes out of locs at the first shampoo anyway
questions.why: Thick gels and residue build up inside locs and may not rinse out. A strand test on a loc shows whether the product washes out, and lighter products or sprays are usually safer; follow the maker's advice for locs.

questions.q: Shantol wants to use the spray at her station. What should she do about the hood dryer next door?
o: Move away from it, or wait until it is off, as heat can ignite the spray
Carry on, as a hood dryer has no naked flame and cannot set off an aerosol can
Spray towards the dryer so that the warm air dries the colour faster
Turn the dryer up so that the spray dries before it reaches the client's skin
questions.why: Aerosol sprays are usually flammable and must be kept away from heat, flames and hot tools, including hood dryers and flat irons. Spraying near heat risks fire and burns.

questions.q: After the wedding Mr. Grant plans to shampoo the colour out. What aftercare advice suits him?
o: Leave the colour in for a week, as locs hold temporary colour well
Use a thick conditioner worked inside the locs to lift the colour out
Brush the colour out of each loc with a stiff brush before washing
Shampoo well, squeeze the locs to rinse them through, and dry fully
questions.why: Locs are rinsed by squeezing so that colour and residue are flushed from the inside, then dried fully so they do not stay damp and smell. Brushing damages locs, and thick conditioner adds residue.

questions.q: How should Ricardo deal with the brown stain in front of the client's ear?
o: Scrub it with a nail brush and warm soapy water until it is gone
Leave it; it will fade on its own by the morning
Dab it with the leftover rinse so that it blends with the hair
Remove it gently with a stain remover, following its instructions
questions.why: Skin stains are removed gently with a stain remover or the maker's wipe, as its instructions say. Scrubbing hurts the skin, and the client should not leave the salon with a visible stain.

questions.q: What should happen to the tint bowl and brush?
o: Rinsed under the tap and left to dry on the counter ready for tomorrow
Put straight into disinfectant with the colour still on them
Washed in warm, soapy water, then disinfected, dried and stored
Wiped with a towel and placed in the UV cabinet overnight
questions.why: Cleaning comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through colour and dirt. Then the tools are disinfected for the contact time, rinsed, dried and stored covered.

questions.q: What is wrong with where the spray can has been left?
o: It is lying under a hot dryer, where heat can make the pressurised can burst
It should be in the fridge, as colour sprays spoil at room temperature
It should be stored with the nozzle down so that the colour does not settle
Nothing, as long as the cap is on and the can is not completely empty
questions.why: Aerosols are stored upright, in a cool place, away from heat, flames and hot tools. Under a running hood dryer the can warms, and a warm pressurised can may burst or catch fire.

questions.q: Rinse has flicked into Ricardo's eye. What should he do first?
o: Rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean, cool running water
Close the eye tightly and wait a few minutes for the stinging to pass
Put a drop of the client's eye make-up remover in the eye to lift the colour
Rub the eye with a clean towel to wipe the colour off the surface
questions.why: Any product in the eye is rinsed at once with plenty of clean, cool water, holding the lid open and not rubbing. If it stays sore or red, he gets medical help, and the accident is recorded.

questions.q: A client's hair was lightened and has gone orange. Which temporary toner would make it look more natural?
o: A violet-based toner
A red-based toner
A blue-based toner
A green-based toner
questions.why: Blue is opposite orange on the colour wheel, so a blue-based product neutralises orange. Violet cancels yellow and green cancels red; red would add more warmth.
